slides.title: The rows you need
slides.main: WHERE keeps only the rows for which the condition is true.

captions: We need part of the table, not all of it, for example only expensive products
After FROM, the word WHERE introduces a condition checked for every row
Rows where the condition is true stay; the data itself does not change

slides.title: Comparisons
slides.main: Equals is one sign =, not equal is <> or !=.

captions: Equality is one sign =, not two as in most languages
Inequality is written <> or !=
Numbers compare by value, strings alphabetically

slides.title: AND, OR, NOT
slides.main: AND needs both conditions, OR at least one, NOT flips the meaning.

captions: AND: a row passes only if both conditions hold
OR: it is enough that at least one holds
NOT flips the meaning of a condition

slides.title: Precedence
slides.main: AND binds tighter than OR; when in doubt, add parentheses.

captions: paid OR shipped AND total > 10000: three conditions in a row, no parentheses
The database reads: paid OR (shipped AND over 10000), so any paid passes
Parentheses around OR give what was meant: status first, then amount

slides.title: IN
slides.main: x IN (…) is shorthand for an OR chain on one column.

captions: Three equalities joined by OR on one column: long
IN with a list in parentheses says the same, shorter
NOT IN keeps values that are not in the list

slides.title: BETWEEN
slides.main: BETWEEN a AND b includes both bounds.

captions: BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000: price from one thousand to five thousand
Both bounds are included: a product at exactly 1200 or 5000 matches too
NOT BETWEEN keeps values outside the range

slides.title: Dates
slides.main: A date in YYYY-MM-DD format compares like an ordinary string.

captions: A date is stored as a "year-month-day" string with leading zeros
Alphabetical order of such strings matches chronological order
BETWEEN works with dates too: all of May 2024

slides.title: LIKE
slides.main: % is any number of characters, _ is exactly one.

captions: % is any sequence, even empty: 'K%' starts with K
'%ov' ends in "ov"; '%uz%' contains "uz"
_ is exactly one character: '_ozlov' finds "Kozlov"

slides.title: Case and NOT LIKE
slides.main: LIKE ignores Latin case; NOT LIKE is negation.

captions: For Latin, LIKE ignores case: 'abc' finds 'ABC' too
For Cyrillic, case matters by default: easy to forget
NOT LIKE is negation; a % sign itself is found via ESCAPE

frames.text: LIKE: Latin case does not matter
ESCAPE sets a special character before %

slides.title: Expressions in a condition
slides.main: A condition can calculate and compare columns with each other.

captions: Price times stock over a hundred thousand: computed for every row
Remainder of dividing by two is zero: even ids
You can compare two columns of one row with each other

slides.title: Order of execution
slides.main: WHERE runs before SELECT, so it cannot see aliases.

captions: FROM takes the table first, then WHERE picks rows, and only then SELECT computes expressions
A SELECT alias is invisible in WHERE: "no such column"
Repeat the whole expression in the condition

slides.title: Building a condition
slides.main: Build a complex condition piece by piece and test each piece.

captions: State the requirement in words: electronics or accessories, over a thousand, in stock
Test each piece with its own query and see how many rows remain
Join the pieces with AND and OR, add parentheses and check the row count

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: WHERE is a condition on rows: comparisons, connectives, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE.

captions: Comparisons, AND/OR/NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE: all combine into one condition
AND beats OR, dates are ISO strings, an alias is invisible in WHERE
Next chapter: row order and LIMIT
